memory_update.text: Treat indium phosphide substrates, probe cards, inspection/metrology, and advanced bonding tools as separate nodes rather than a single generic 'semicap' bucket.
Treat sulphuric acid logistics and regeneration as a distinct bottleneck layer for copper SX-EW and HPAL, not just as a commodity chemistry input.
Treat electrical contracting, custom power systems, and switchgear as a monetizable AI-data-center implementation layer, not merely a utility proxy.
Export permits and customer qualification can be the actual chokepoint in substrate and specialty-material chains even when physical capacity exists.
The 2026 sulphur/sulphuric acid shock is a live catalyst that can rapidly move second-order names in chemicals, logistics, and mining feedstocks.

Need direct primary-source verification from company filings and earnings transcripts for backlog size, capacity additions, and customer concentration in AXTI, CAMT, KLIC, POWL, IESC, ECVT, HWKN, ALM, KMT, and ELMT.
AXTI is the clearest primary chokepoint name in this chunk because its revenue and shipments are tied to InP substrate export permits, making it both demand-exposed and policy-constrained.
CAMT and KLIC sit one step downstream of the HBM story and should be treated as equipment/inspection leverage rather than raw-material bottlenecks.
ALM, KMT, and ELMT form a separate tungsten-critical-minerals cluster; ALM is the cleaner upstream supply expression, while KMT and ELMT are downstream conversion / component names.
POWL belongs to the AI power buildout lane and should not be conflated with semiconductor or materials bottlenecks.
TGB, ECVT, and HWKN are second-order sulphuric-acid chain exposures; the main falsification risk is that they benefit only transiently or not at all if feedstock pricing normalizes.
Need primary-source verification from filings, earnings calls, investor presentations, and government export-control documents before promoting any narrative proxy to a durable thesis.

New Hotspots Layer 2B is anchored by three visible relationship clusters: AI data-center liquid cooling, AI grid/electrical buildout, and HBM/advanced packaging. Reference leaders VRT, ETN, AMKR, COHR, and LITE define the obvious lane; underfollowed names NVT, MOD, STRL, MYRG, KLIC, CAMT, and AXTI are the primary candidates to verify for hidden revenue concentration and bottleneck exposure.

Need primary-source verification of revenue mix and customer qualification for liquid cooling at NVT and MOD, backlog composition for STRL and MYRG, and InP customer/supplier relationships for AXTI, COHR, and LITE.

AMSC should remain in the underfollowed grid-power lane only as an inference until Comtrafo's transformer voltage classes, U.S. availability, data-center utility exposure, and backlog contribution are verified from primary sources.
COHR is a reference leader, not an underfollowed candidate, for the InP optical-interconnect lane; use it to benchmark InP substrate scarcity, vertical integration, and downstream optical demand.

ONTO belongs in the HBM/advanced-packaging process-control lane, but the key survival test is whether advanced-packaging revenue is tied to HBM/AI accelerator ramps rather than a broad semiconductor capex recovery.

DOV and WTS are second-order liquid-cooling component candidates where strategic relevance may exceed financial materiality; later layers must quantify CPC or data-center cooling revenue contribution before ranking.

AEHR should be kept as a speculative shadow candidate: the AI/HBM thesis requires evidence that an AI processor evaluation customer has converted to volume production and that the tools are used in the relevant reliability-test flow.
POET is a speculative optical-engine candidate; require named customers, committed volume orders, production revenue, and InP sourcing validation before it can move beyond hypothesis.
CC is a speculative immersion-cooling-fluid option, but direct-to-chip liquid cooling, PFAS/regulatory exposure, and lack of commercial contract evidence are major falsification vectors.

FCX should be retained as a sulphuric-acid/copper SX-EW reference anchor rather than an underfollowed candidate; the investable underfollowed hunt should move toward acid producers, distributors, logistics, and regional substitute supply.
Need live market-cap, liquidity, valuation, analyst coverage, and primary-source exposure checks for every candidate before Layer 3 prioritization.

Need direct primary-source evidence from 10-K/10-Q filings, earnings calls, investor presentations, product catalogs, customer certifications, and capacity/backlog disclosures; current chunk evidence is sufficient for relationship mapping but not for ranking conviction.

KEX maps to the sulphur/sulphuric-acid hotspot only as an indirect chemical-logistics hypothesis; next layer must verify actual sulphuric-acid or acid-adjacent cargo exposure and pricing/utilization sensitivity.

THR maps to AI liquid-cooling infrastructure as a testing/commissioning hypothesis rather than direct cooling hardware; survival requires proof of commercial liquid-cooled load-bank or data-center temperature-management orders.
PLPC maps to AI power/grid stress through utility T&D hardware and substation connectors; company-specific evidence must show accelerating utility order demand in data-center-heavy regions.
MTSI maps to the InP hotspot as an adjacent photonics semiconductor candidate; key unknowns are InP product materiality, optical-interconnect exposure, and substrate sourcing constraints.
AAOI maps downstream of InP through optical transceivers, but the claim is speculative until laser technology, InP use, AI customer demand, and substrate shortage sensitivity are verified.
IE and VALE are more likely acid-cost sensitivity checks than clean beneficiaries; the node is useful for falsifying sulphuric-acid bottleneck impact on copper/nickel economics.

ATI, ATALF, and GMTL map to tungsten/defense-material supply, but ATI requires tungsten revenue verification and ATALF/GMTL should remain speculative micro-cap/developer exceptions until permitting, funding, processing, and customer validation evidence improves.

summary: Split Layer 2 synthesis. Layer 2A map for 'New Hotspots' focuses on three live bottleneck clusters that emerged from the cached Serenity universe: AI data-center power buildout, HBM/advanced packaging, and critical-mineral feedstocks (especially tungsten and sulphuric acid). The industry-chain map deliberately emphasizes lower-attention suppliers, distributors, certification gates, and regulated inputs rather than mega-cap end demand. Catalysts are mostly capacity, customer, policy, and pricing shocks that can re-rate the scarce layers first.

supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: The headline demand driver for new hotspots is the continued buildout of AI compute, which pulls through data-center power gear, semiconductors, advanced packaging, optics, and special materials.

This is where AI demand becomes real orders for electrical infrastructure, switchgear, transformers, power controls, and installation labor. It is a demand node, but also the place where project timing and utility interconnect delays can create bottlenecks.

supply_chain_map.node: Grid interconnection, transformers, switchgear, packaged power systems
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: These are scarce implementation layers for data-center expansion. Capacity constraints, long lead times, and backlog conversion can make this one of the first monetizable chokepoints in AI infrastructure.

supply_chain_map.node: Electrical contracting and custom power installation
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Project execution, labor availability, and subcontractor capacity can become limiting factors even when end demand is strong. This layer can capture bottleneck value without being a classic semiconductor or software beneficiary.

HBM adoption and advanced packaging complexity drive demand for inspection, metrology, probing, bonding, and assembly equipment. This layer is closer to the real manufacturing constraint than generic AI chip names.

Yield sensitivity rises with tighter interconnects, higher density packages, and more complex memory stacks. These tools can become gating items because customers must qualify them before volume ramps.

supply_chain_map.node: Advanced bonding / back-end semiconductor assembly tools
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: As packaging moves toward tighter pitch and heterogeneous integration, bonding tools can shift from niche to chokepoint. Qualification cycles and repeat order visibility matter more than headline TAM.

A critical upstream input for optical interconnects and laser components. Supply is constrained by export controls, limited producers, and customer-specific qualification, making it a classic low-attention chokepoint.

Downstream of InP wafers, this layer converts scarce substrate supply into AI interconnect hardware. Demand is strong, but the bottleneck often starts upstream in substrate supply and then propagates downstream.

A hidden but critical feedstock for copper SX-EW and nickel HPAL. In 2026 the acid market became structurally tighter due to trade disruption and export controls, pushing this node into bottleneck territory.

supply_chain_map.node: Copper SX-EW and nickel HPAL operations
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: These miners/processors are highly sensitive to acid availability. HPAL in particular can be an on/off process, so feedstock shortages can quickly translate into output cuts.

Tungsten is strategically important for defense, hardmetals, and precision industrial components. Supply concentration and export restrictions can support non-China supply chains and create pricing power for qualified converters.
These are second-order beneficiaries of tungsten tightness. They are not always obvious to market screens, but qualification and materials control can make them scarce capacity nodes.
Export permits, trade controls, and customer qualification can be the actual bottleneck even when physical capacity exists. This is especially important for InP wafers and strategic minerals.

supply_chain_map.node: Specialty chemicals distributors and acid logistics
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Distribution, storage, and transport can hide value in supply shocks. These firms may not screen as obvious commodity beneficiaries, but they can capture margin or become chokepoints when regional supply tightens.
